Part of #1. Reopens #30; lever 1 of #1587.

## Problem

- **The reviewer is most of what auto mode costs.** After #1471 it was 12–24% of each canary job's cost (#1587, 2026-10-11). Each review is a model round trip: stage one takes 2.0–2.4 s median and 4.9–6.5 s p95, and reads 10–12k input tokens (`research/decision-models/README.md`, "Fiber's reviewer on imported sessions"). In switchyard#204's canary, 104 of the 114 reviewed calls would have run unharmed in a workspace-and-temp, no-network sandbox, and none was denied.
- **Nothing limits a call once it runs.** The credential deny sees declared paths only, so `python -c` opening `credentials/` is stopped by the reviewer alone. A shell call can also reach Fiber's own sockets, through which any client can start a session or answer a permission request.

#1587's ruling kept #30 on that data. Ruling 12 reopens it as an opt-in sandbox, default off. The opening question is whether commands that run inside it skip the reviewer.

## What the docs say

- `docs/permissions.md:187-190`: "Fiber does not confine what a tool call can reach at the operating-system level ... nothing limits what it does once it runs."
- `docs/permissions.md:109-138`: the fast paths are reads, workspace writes outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`, Markdown in data directories, and network calls to known hosts. "Everything else — shell execution ... — is reviewed."
- `docs/invocation.md:1159-1160` ("Remote clients"): "a session's shell reaches the local socket". `docs/permissions.md:536-539`: "any driver replies to it identically".
- `docs/configuration.md:79-81`: a repository "never sets a key that widens what runs without asking".

## The opening question: yes, for what the sandbox contains

The sandbox was measured on macOS 27.0 (Seatbelt) and Linux 6.8 (Landlock ABI 4, in Docker), alongside Claude Code's sandbox-runtime (srt) 0.0.81 and codex 0.163.0. A shell call inside the proposed sandbox (Option A below):

| can | cannot |
|---|---|
| read any file except Fiber home's `credentials/` and a person's extra denies | write outside the workspace and temp, directly or through a grandchild, `python -c` or a symlink |
| write the workspace and temp | write `.git/hooks/`, `.git/config`, a worktree's `.git` file or `.fiber/` (macOS; Linux is Q5) |
| commit in a delegate's worktree, whose git directory is outside the workspace | open any socket: no internet, no DNS, no localhost TCP, no Unix socket (so no hub, session socket, `docker.sock` or ssh-agent) |
| run and build (`cargo build` with a warm registry) | signal a process outside it (macOS; Linux from Landlock ABI 6), or ask launchd to run anything |

Each "can" is already a fast path, apart from temp writes: the read fast path reads any file except `credentials/`, and the workspace fast path writes any workspace file outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`. So **a confined call skips the reviewer as a new fast path**. The credential deny and the person's standing deny and ask rules still come first and still apply.

**Still reviewed:**

- a shell call the model marks `unconfined`, which is how it leaves the sandbox. It is judged exactly as today.
- network calls: `gh`, `git push`/`fetch`, `curl`, package installs. A domain allowlist would not contain them: allowing `github.com` allows a push to any repository, as srt's own README warns.
- writes outside the workspace: harness configuration, `~/.cargo` on a cold cache, the npm cache.
- MCP and extension tool calls, because the server or extension runs outside any shell sandbox. Codex starts MCP servers unsandboxed too (`research/sandbox/reference-agents.md`, §7).
- `delegate_*` (always reviewed), web fetches to unknown hosts, and file-tool writes outside the workspace. These are unchanged.

**How many reviews it saves.** Measured: 91% (104 of 114) in delegate lanes. Estimated: 65–83% of reviewed shell calls in the owner's interactive pi and Claude Code sessions, computed as (P − R) / (1 − R) from `research/sandbox/usage.md` (P, the share of calls that run unharmed in the sandbox) and #1497's sweep (R, the share of calls that are read-only). The two sweeps have different dates, so the second figure is an estimate. What remains is mostly `gh` and `git push`/`fetch`.

**What skipping review gives up.** Destruction inside the workspace (`rm -rf src/`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fdx`) runs unreviewed, and unlike an edit, it cannot be undone from the session log. Codex's workspace-write and Claude Code accept this: Claude Code's `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` "still defaults to true" in 2.1.304. See Q3.

**Recommendation: A.** It is the only option that starts wherever Fiber ships (`docs/releasing.md`: macOS arm64, Linux musl), and it costs milliseconds and no memory. It needs no proxy because it allows no network, and every network call stays reviewed anyway. B's domain allowlist is the one thing A lacks, and it would not let `gh` or `git push` skip review. C is A's macOS half plus a Linux path that does not start on the hosts measured.

**Failure goes toward review.** When the sandbox cannot be applied (no Landlock, an old kernel, a missing `sandbox-exec`), calls do not declare `confined` and are reviewed as today, and the session says so once. A call declared `confined` never runs unconfined: if applying the sandbox fails at spawn, the call fails.

## What it means for Fiber's own processes

- **One spawn site.** Foreground and backgrounded shell commands both spawn at `crates/tools/src/shell/command.rs:131`. The sandbox wraps that spawn.
- **Delegate worktrees.** A worktree's git directory is `<repo>/.git/worktrees/<id>`, outside the workspace. srt and codex both fail `git commit` there (measured). A grants the worktree's git directory and the shared `objects/`, `refs/` and `logs/`, and denies `hooks/`, `config` and the worktree's `.git` file. Commits work on both platforms (measured). Repointing the `.git` file would make the next unconfined `git` read a config the call wrote, which is why A denies it. Granting all of `refs/` lets a delegate move other branches (Q6).
- **Fiber's sockets** (`~/.fiber/run/`). A blocks every Unix socket on both platforms (measured). Two alternatives do not:
  - codex with `network_access=true`: the stand-in hub socket answered (measured).
  - bubblewrap's `--unshare-net` alone: a pathname socket ignores network namespaces, so `run/` must also be hidden (measured).
- **Not confined, unchanged:** `host.exec`, MCP stdio servers (`crates/mcp/src/server.rs:267`), process extensions, image and PDF children, delegates (`crates/jobs/src/delegate.rs:785`), Fiber's own worktree `git` (`crates/worktree/src/lib.rs:336`), and the hub's session spawns. The calls that reach them are reviewed as today.
- **`tty: true`.** A deny-default profile refuses ioctls on the inherited pty, so `stty` fails. One rule fixes it (measured).
- **The built-in `grep`** writes its side file in `$TMPDIR` (`crates/tools/src/shell/matches.rs:16`), so A keeps `$TMPDIR` writable. srt's temp policy, which allows only `/tmp/claude`, would break it.
- **`ps` and `pgrep`** fail inside every Seatbelt sandbox measured, Fiber's, srt's and codex's: `sandbox-exec` refuses to exec a setuid binary, and `sysmond` is unreachable (Q4).

## Ruling: Linux read denies are built by enumerating ancestors (option A, with four corrections)

The contract stands: a confined shell reads everything except Fiber's credentials and the `sandbox.deny_read` paths, on Linux as on macOS. Option C would weaken the one protection the owner chose the sandbox for, on the platform that carries the usage. Option B needs unprivileged user namespaces, which Ubuntu 24.04 restricts, and a mechanism Q10 did not admit. Option D is impossible. That leaves A, built with Landlock alone.

**The mechanism.** At each confined spawn, for every denied path, Fiber walks from `/` towards it. For each existing ancestor directory on the way, it grants read on every entry except the one leading to the denied path. A directory gets a subtree grant and a file gets a file grant. The denied path itself gets nothing. Entries created in an enumerated ancestor during the call are unreadable until the next call. That fails closed.

**Corrections to the option as written:**

1. **A missing component stops the walk; it does not move the deny point up.** Treating the nearest existing ancestor as the deny point would deny all of `~` whenever `~/.aws` does not exist. Instead, the walk stops at the first missing component, and nothing is granted for it. If it is created later, it is a new entry in an enumerated directory and so unreadable. Nothing is lost, and nothing is over-denied.
2. **Never follow a symlink while building grants.** Open entries with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW`. A symlink entry gets no grant of its own. Landlock judges an access through a symlink by the target's resolved path, so the link reaches whatever its target is granted. Without this rule, a link in `~` pointing at `~/.ssh` would be opened as `~/.ssh` and granted.
3. **A denied path inside a write grant is a configuration error.** A write grant is a subtree grant, so it would re-grant reads beneath a denied path inside it. A `deny_read` path inside the workspace, the temp directory or any `allow_write` path therefore makes the sandbox unavailable for the session. One notice names the path, and the session falls back to ordinary review, as for a non-empty `allow_unix_sockets`. Fiber's credentials live in Fiber home, outside every write grant, so they always hold.
4. **Hard links are out of scope.** A hard link elsewhere to a denied file reads as that other path, on both platforms. `docs/sandbox.md` says so in one line.

**Docs (slice 1's docs commit, `docs/sandbox.md`, Linux).** State that the read set is built at spawn by enumerating the ancestors of each denied path, that entries created in those directories during a call stay unreadable until the next call, and corrections 1 to 4.

**Fence.** Yes, the walk is a helper in `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/`, already in the fence. Tests cover a denied file under `~`, with a sibling readable, a symlink to it, a missing deny path then created mid-call, and a deny path inside the workspace refused.

**Cost.** Memory is measured with the dependency measurement already required, and recorded in `docs/dependencies.md`. Spawn time adds no `docs/performance.md` row, since no shell-spawn row exists and a row needs a bench entry. The PR reports the rule count and the walk's time on Linux for the owner's home directory. If it is over a millisecond, it gets a ticket for a timing row.

## Owner rulings

Owner rulings (2026-10-21), all eleven questions. Q1 was posted above; it is repeated here so every answer is in one place.

- Q1: yes. A shell call that runs confined skips the reviewer, as a new fast path after the credential deny and the person's standing deny and ask rules.
- Q2: option A. Fiber writes its own policy on Seatbelt (macOS) and Landlock plus seccomp (Linux); no srt, no bubblewrap.
- Q3: keep a built-in destructive list reviewed even when confined: `rm -r`/`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, `git checkout --`, `git restore`. It matches any part of a multi-part command (unlike a standing ask rule), is checked before the confined fast path, and is best effort by command text.
- Q4: yes. With the sandbox on, read-only fast-path calls also run confined (#53's joining rule), so a wrong `shell.read_only` entry fails instead of writing. `ps` and `pgrep` fail on macOS and use the Q7 escape.
- Q5: an after-call check on Linux. Before a confined call Fiber records `.git/config`, the hooks directory, a worktree's `.git` file and `.fiber/`; after it, Fiber restores any change and reports it in the call's result. Main checkouts and worktrees are both confined.
- Q6: a confined delegate is granted all of `refs/`. A local branch moved by mistake is recovered from the reflog; `git push` stays reviewed.
- Q7: an `unconfined: true` argument on the shell tool, set by the model per call. An unconfined call is reviewed exactly as with the sandbox off. Fiber never reruns a failed confined call by itself.
- Q8: the `sandbox.*` keys are person-only, set in global config or with `-c`; a repository's project config cannot turn the sandbox on. A delegate inherits its parent's setting. Toggling changes the shell tool's description, a person-initiated prompt-cache miss, which is acceptable.

- Q11: yes. "Sandbox" names the feature and its keys; "confined" names a call that ran inside it.

## Ruling: Linux read denies are built by enumerating ancestors (option A, with four corrections)

The contract stands: a confined shell reads everything except Fiber's credentials and the `sandbox.deny_read` paths, on Linux as on macOS. Option C would weaken the one protection the owner chose the sandbox for, on the platform that carries the usage. Option B needs unprivileged user namespaces, which Ubuntu 24.04 restricts, and a mechanism Q10 did not admit. Option D is impossible. That leaves A, built with Landlock alone.

**The mechanism.** At each confined spawn, for every denied path, Fiber walks from `/` towards it. For each existing ancestor directory on the way, it grants read on every entry except the one leading to the denied path. A directory gets a subtree grant and a file gets a file grant. The denied path itself gets nothing. Entries created in an enumerated ancestor during the call are unreadable until the next call. That fails closed.

**Corrections to the option as written:**

1. **A missing component stops the walk; it does not move the deny point up.** Treating the nearest existing ancestor as the deny point would deny all of `~` whenever `~/.aws` does not exist. Instead, the walk stops at the first missing component, and nothing is granted for it. If it is created later, it is a new entry in an enumerated directory and so unreadable. Nothing is lost, and nothing is over-denied.
2. **Never follow a symlink while building grants.** Open entries with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW`. A symlink entry gets no grant of its own. Landlock judges an access through a symlink by the target's resolved path, so the link reaches whatever its target is granted. Without this rule, a link in `~` pointing at `~/.ssh` would be opened as `~/.ssh` and granted.
3. **A denied path inside a write grant is a configuration error.** A write grant is a subtree grant, so it would re-grant reads beneath a denied path inside it. A `deny_read` path inside the workspace, the temp directory or any `allow_write` path therefore makes the sandbox unavailable for the session. One notice names the path, and the session falls back to ordinary review, as for a non-empty `allow_unix_sockets`. Fiber's credentials live in Fiber home, outside every write grant, so they always hold.
4. **Hard links are out of scope.** A hard link elsewhere to a denied file reads as that other path, on both platforms. `docs/sandbox.md` says so in one line.

**Docs (slice 1's docs commit, `docs/sandbox.md`, Linux).** State that the read set is built at spawn by enumerating the ancestors of each denied path, that entries created in those directories during a call stay unreadable until the next call, and corrections 1 to 4.

**Fence.** Yes, the walk is a helper in `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/`, already in the fence. Tests cover a denied file under `~`, with a sibling readable, a symlink to it, a missing deny path then created mid-call, and a deny path inside the workspace refused.

**Cost.** Memory is measured with the dependency measurement already required, and recorded in `docs/dependencies.md`. Spawn time adds no `docs/performance.md` row, since no shell-spawn row exists and a row needs a bench entry. The PR reports the rule count and the walk's time on Linux for the owner's home directory. If it is over a millisecond, it gets a ticket for a timing row.

Slice 1 is Linux-only: landlock and seccompiler, ABI floor 2, deny sockets, no sandbox.allow_unix_sockets. No shims or edits to existing command pins. Preserve the event semantics: tool_call_started precedes execution; confined calls carry confined:true, including spawn failure; policy-apply failure runs no command and never retries unconfined. ## Full code review findings

P1 `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/mod.rs:231` — Landlock grants from each deny path are unioned. Walking the Fiber credentials path grants sibling directories under `~`, including a separate `sandbox.deny_read` subtree such as `~/.aws`; it can be read despite the extra deny. Build the ancestor grants against the union of all denied paths, omitting every entry that leads to any denied path.
P1 `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/mod.rs:210` — The walk breaks before enumerating the denied path's parent. It must grant readable siblings in that parent, then stop at the denied or missing component, without moving a missing deny point upward. This also preserves readable siblings when `~/.aws` does not exist.
P2 `crates/tools/src/shell/command.rs:207` — `effects` and spawn call `check_available` separately. If reload turns the sandbox off after `tool_call_started` declares `confined: true`, spawn can run unconfined. Carry the declared per-call sandbox decision into spawn; when a confined decision can no longer be applied, fail the call without running it or retrying unconfined.

{"body":"
Part of #1. Reopens #30; lever 1 of #1587.

## Problem

- **The reviewer is most of what auto mode costs.** After #1471 it was 12–24% of each canary job's cost (#1587, 2026-10-11). Each review is a model round trip: stage one takes 2.0–2.4 s median and 4.9–6.5 s p95, and reads 10–12k input tokens (`research/decision-models/README.md`, "Fiber's reviewer on imported sessions"). In switchyard#204's canary, 104 of the 114 reviewed calls would have run unharmed in a workspace-and-temp, no-network sandbox, and none was denied.
- **Nothing limits a call once it runs.** The credential deny sees declared paths only, so `python -c` opening `credentials/` is stopped by the reviewer alone. A shell call can also reach Fiber's own sockets, through which any client can start a session or answer a permission request.

#1587's ruling kept #30 on that data. Ruling 12 reopens it as an opt-in sandbox, default off. The opening question is whether commands that run inside it skip the reviewer.

## What the docs say

- `docs/permissions.md:187-190`: "Fiber does not confine what a tool call can reach at the operating-system level ... nothing limits what it does once it runs."
- `docs/permissions.md:109-138`: the fast paths are reads, workspace writes outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`, Markdown in data directories, and network calls to known hosts. "Everything else — shell execution ... — is reviewed."
- `docs/invocation.md:1159-1160` ("Remote clients"): "a session's shell reaches the local socket". `docs/permissions.md:536-539`: "any driver replies to it identically".
- `docs/configuration.md:79-81`: a repository "never sets a key that widens what runs without asking".

## The opening question: yes, for what the sandbox contains

The sandbox was measured on macOS 27.0 (Seatbelt) and Linux 6.8 (Landlock ABI 4, in Docker), alongside Claude Code's sandbox-runtime (srt) 0.0.81 and codex 0.163.0. A shell call inside the proposed sandbox (Option A below):

| can | cannot |
|---|---|
| read any file except Fiber home's `credentials/` and a person's extra denies | write outside the workspace and temp, directly or through a grandchild, `python -c` or a symlink |
| write the workspace and temp | write `.git/hooks/`, `.git/config`, a worktree's `.git` file or `.fiber/` (macOS; Linux is Q5) |
| commit in a delegate's worktree, whose git directory is outside the workspace | open any socket: no internet, no DNS, no localhost TCP, no Unix socket (so no hub, session socket, `docker.sock` or ssh-agent) |
| run and build (`cargo build` with a warm registry) | signal a process outside it (macOS; Linux from Landlock ABI 6), or ask launchd to run anything |

Each "can" is already a fast path, apart from temp writes: the read fast path reads any file except `credentials/`, and the workspace fast path writes any workspace file outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`. So **a confined call skips the reviewer as a new fast path**. The credential deny and the person's standing deny and ask rules still come first and still apply.

**Still reviewed:**

- a shell call the model marks `unconfined`, which is how it leaves the sandbox. It is judged exactly as today.
- network calls: `gh`, `git push`/`fetch`, `curl`, package installs. A domain allowlist would not contain them: allowing `github.com` allows a push to any repository, as srt's own README warns.
- writes outside the workspace: harness configuration, `~/.cargo` on a cold cache, the npm cache.
- MCP and extension tool calls, because the server or extension runs outside any shell sandbox. Codex starts MCP servers unsandboxed too (`research/sandbox/reference-agents.md`, §7).
- `delegate_*` (always reviewed), web fetches to unknown hosts, and file-tool writes outside the workspace. These are unchanged.

**How many reviews it saves.** Measured: 91% (104 of 114) in delegate lanes. Estimated: 65–83% of reviewed shell calls in the owner's interactive pi and Claude Code sessions, computed as (P − R) / (1 − R) from `research/sandbox/usage.md` (P, the share of calls that run unharmed in the sandbox) and #1497's sweep (R, the share of calls that are read-only). The two sweeps have different dates, so the second figure is an estimate. What remains is mostly `gh` and `git push`/`fetch`.

**What skipping review gives up.** Destruction inside the workspace (`rm -rf src/`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fdx`) runs unreviewed, and unlike an edit, it cannot be undone from the session log. Codex's workspace-write and Claude Code accept this: Claude Code's `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` "still defaults to true" in 2.1.304. See Q3.

## Options

| | **A. Fiber's own policy** (recommended) | **B. srt** | **C. bubblewrap on Linux** (codex's way) |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS | Seatbelt profile run through `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` | srt's Seatbelt profile plus an HTTP/SOCKS proxy | Seatbelt, as in A |
| Linux | Landlock plus a seccomp filter, applied in the shell's `pre_exec` | bubblewrap, socat, ripgrep, a seccomp helper, the proxy | bubblewrap with namespaces, plus seccomp |
| Added per call (median) | macOS +6 to +12 ms (the higher under load); Linux +0.3 to +0.8 ms | CLI: +100 to +184 ms (macOS). As a library: +14 ms, inside Node | Linux +1.9 ms |
| Resident while a call runs | nothing (the wrapper execs) | CLI: 76 MiB of Node per call. Library: an 85 MiB Node sidecar. Fiber's whole tree is ~35 MiB | 3.2 MiB per running command (two `bwrap` processes) |
| Starts on Ubuntu 24.04, in Docker, on GitHub's runners | yes: Landlock needs no user namespace (ABI 4 in Docker here, ABI 7 on the runners in #30) | no: failed in every Docker mode tried, and fails closed | no: needs capability-bearing user namespaces, which `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1` and Docker's default profile refuse. Codex fails closed, so every command fails |
| Network allowlist | none: no sockets at all | yes, by domain | none, or a proxy as in B |
| Protects `.git/config`, hooks, `.fiber/` and a worktree's `.git` file | macOS: yes. Linux: no, because Landlock only grants, so a writable workspace includes them (Q5) | no `.fiber/`. On macOS the worktree's `.git` file stayed writable (measured); srt guards it on Linux only | yes (read-only binds) |
| New dependencies | macOS none; Linux `landlock` and `seccompiler`, or about 200 lines over `libc` (Q10) | Node ≥ 22.12 on the person's machine | a `bwrap` binary, installed or bundled |

**Recommendation: A.** It is the only option that starts wherever Fiber ships (`docs/releasing.md`: macOS arm64, Linux musl), and it costs milliseconds and no memory. It needs no proxy because it allows no network, and every network call stays reviewed anyway. B's domain allowlist is the one thing A lacks, and it would not let `gh` or `git push` skip review. C is A's macOS half plus a Linux path that does not start on the hosts measured.

**Failure goes toward review.** When the sandbox cannot be applied (no Landlock, an old kernel, a missing `sandbox-exec`), calls do not declare `confined` and are reviewed as today, and the session says so once. A call declared `confined` never runs unconfined: if applying the sandbox fails at spawn, the call fails.

## What it means for Fiber's own processes

- **One spawn site.** Foreground and backgrounded shell commands both spawn at `crates/tools/src/shell/command.rs:131`. The sandbox wraps that spawn.
- **Delegate worktrees.** A worktree's git directory is `<repo>/.git/worktrees/<id>`, outside the workspace. srt and codex both fail `git commit` there (measured). A grants the worktree's git directory and the shared `objects/`, `refs/` and `logs/`, and denies `hooks/`, `config` and the worktree's `.git` file. Commits work on both platforms (measured). Repointing the `.git` file would make the next unconfined `git` read a config the call wrote, which is why A denies it. Granting all of `refs/` lets a delegate move other branches (Q6).
- **Fiber's sockets** (`~/.fiber/run/`). A blocks every Unix socket on both platforms (measured). Two alternatives do not:
  - codex with `network_access=true`: the stand-in hub socket answered (measured).
  - bubblewrap's `--unshare-net` alone: a pathname socket ignores network namespaces, so `run/` must also be hidden (measured).
- **Not confined, unchanged:** `host.exec`, MCP stdio servers (`crates/mcp/src/server.rs:267`), process extensions, image and PDF children, delegates (`crates/jobs/src/delegate.rs:785`), Fiber's own worktree `git` (`crates/worktree/src/lib.rs:336`), and the hub's session spawns. The calls that reach them are reviewed as today.
- **`tty: true`.** A deny-default profile refuses ioctls on the inherited pty, so `stty` fails. One rule fixes it (measured).
- **The built-in `grep`** writes its side file in `$TMPDIR` (`crates/tools/src/shell/matches.rs:16`), so A keeps `$TMPDIR` writable. srt's temp policy, which allows only `/tmp/claude`, would break it.
- **`ps` and `pgrep`** fail inside every Seatbelt sandbox measured, Fiber's, srt's and codex's: `sandbox-exec` refuses to exec a setuid binary, and `sysmond` is unreachable (Q4).

## The owner's own sessions

- **Off (the default):** nothing changes.
- **On:** an edit to harness configuration or credentials fails inside the sandbox. The model reruns it with `unconfined: true`, which is reviewed exactly as today, so it is never worse than off. `sandbox.allow_write` adds paths, such as `~/.pi/agent` or `~/.claude`, so those edits stay confined and unreviewed. `sandbox.deny_read` adds read denies.
- The sandbox's own read deny is whatever the credential deny covers: Fiber home's `credentials/`, `file` sources, and whatever #3025 adds.
- Every `sandbox.*` key is person-only, because turning it on widens what runs without asking.

## Docs that change (docs first)

- `docs/permissions.md`: "Confinement" is rewritten. "Fast paths" gains the confined path. "Effects" gains the `confined` qualifier. "Credentials" (`:157`, "Fiber does not confine tools") and "Delegates" change to match.
- `docs/tools.md`: "Shell" gains the `unconfined` argument, and `:697-698` ("Fiber does not confine the shell") changes. "Effects" and "What a tool declares" gain `confined`.
- `docs/events.md`: "Declared effects" gains `confined` (boolean, omitted when false), so the log shows which calls ran confined.
- `docs/configuration.md`: the person-only keys `sandbox.enabled`, `sandbox.allow_write`, `sandbox.deny_read` and `sandbox.allow_unix_sockets`. The last never accepts `run/`.
- `docs/invocation.md:1159-1160` gains "unless the sandbox is on".
- `docs/delegates.md`: worktree commits inside the sandbox, and whether a delegate inherits the setting.
- `docs/dependencies.md`: the Linux crates, if Q10 picks them.
- `GLOSSARY.md`: "sandbox", and "confined" for a call that runs in it (Q11).
- The platform mechanics go in a new `docs/sandbox.md`, as #30's "Output" anticipated, or into "Confinement" (Q9).
- The probe scripts and results go in `research/sandbox/opt-in/`.

## Rulings this reopens

- #30 (`docs/permissions.md`, "Confinement").
- #1587 lever 1, owner 2026-10-11: "don't build a sandbox. #30 stands."
- Not "One mode": confinement adds a fast path, not a mode, as `shell.read_only` does. #2419 (no reviewer at all) stays separate.

2. Option A, B or C?

## Owner rulings

Owner rulings (2026-10-21), all eleven questions. Q1 was posted above; it is repeated here so every answer is in one place.

- Q1: yes. A shell call that runs confined skips the reviewer, as a new fast path after the credential deny and the person's standing deny and ask rules.
- Q2: option A. Fiber writes its own policy on Seatbelt (macOS) and Landlock plus seccomp (Linux); no srt, no bubblewrap.
- Q3: keep a built-in destructive list reviewed even when confined: `rm -r`/`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, `git checkout --`, `git restore`. ## Ruling: Linux read denies are built by enumerating ancestors (option A, with four corrections)

The contract stands: a confined shell reads everything except Fiber's credentials and the `sandbox.deny_read` paths, on Linux as on macOS. Option C would weaken the one protection the owner chose the sandbox for, on the platform that carries the usage. Option B needs unprivileged user namespaces, which Ubuntu 24.04 restricts, and a mechanism Q10 did not admit. Option D is impossible. That leaves A, built with Landlock alone.

**The mechanism.** At each confined spawn, for every denied path, Fiber walks from `/` towards it. For each existing ancestor directory on the way, it grants read on every entry except the one leading to the denied path. A directory gets a subtree grant and a file gets a file grant. The denied path itself gets nothing. Entries created in an enumerated ancestor during the call are unreadable until the next call. That fails closed.

**Corrections to the option as written:**

1. **A missing component stops the walk; it does not move the deny point up.** Treating the nearest existing ancestor as the deny point would deny all of `~` whenever `~/.aws` does not exist. Instead, the walk stops at the first missing component, and nothing is granted for it. If it is created later, it is a new entry in an enumerated directory and so unreadable. Nothing is lost, and nothing is over-denied.
2. **Never follow a symlink while building grants.** Open entries with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW`. A symlink entry gets no grant of its own. Landlock judges an access through a symlink by the target's resolved path, so the link reaches whatever its target is granted. Without this rule, a link in `~` pointing at `~/.ssh` would be opened as `~/.ssh` and granted.
3. **A denied path inside a write grant is a configuration error.** A write grant is a subtree grant, so it would re-grant reads beneath a denied path inside it. A `deny_read` path inside the workspace, the temp directory or any `allow_write` path therefore makes the sandbox unavailable for the session. One notice names the path, and the session falls back to ordinary review, as for a non-empty `allow_unix_sockets`. Fiber's credentials live in Fiber home, outside every write grant, so they always hold.
4. **Hard links are out of scope.** A hard link elsewhere to a denied file reads as that other path, on both platforms. `docs/sandbox.md` says so in one line.

**Docs (slice 1's docs commit, `docs/sandbox.md`, Linux).** State that the read set is built at spawn by enumerating the ancestors of each denied path, that entries created in those directories during a call stay unreadable until the next call, and corrections 1 to 4.

**Fence.** Yes, the walk is a helper in `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/`, already in the fence. Tests cover a denied file under `~`, with a sibling readable, a symlink to it, a missing deny path then created mid-call, and a deny path inside the workspace refused.

**Cost.** Memory is measured with the dependency measurement already required, and recorded in `docs/dependencies.md`. Part of #1. Reopens #30; lever 1 of #1587.

## Problem

- **The reviewer is most of what auto mode costs.** After #1471 it was 12–24% of each canary job's cost (#1587, 2026-10-11). Each review is a model round trip: stage one takes 2.0–2.4 s median and 4.9–6.5 s p95, and reads 10–12k input tokens (`research/decision-models/README.md`, "Fiber's reviewer on imported sessions"). In switchyard#204's canary, 104 of the 114 reviewed calls would have run unharmed in a workspace-and-temp, no-network sandbox, and none was denied.
- **Nothing limits a call once it runs.** The credential deny sees declared paths only, so `python -c` opening `credentials/` is stopped by the reviewer alone. A shell call can also reach Fiber's own sockets, through which any client can start a session or answer a permission request.

#1587's ruling kept #30 on that data. Ruling 12 reopens it as an opt-in sandbox, default off. The opening question is whether commands that run inside it skip the reviewer.

## What the docs say

- `docs/permissions.md:187-190`: "Fiber does not confine what a tool call can reach at the operating-system level ... nothing limits what it does once it runs."
- `docs/permissions.md:109-138`: the fast paths are reads, workspace writes outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`, Markdown in data directories, and network calls to known hosts. "Everything else — shell execution ... — is reviewed."
- `docs/invocation.md:1159-1160` ("Remote clients"): "a session's shell reaches the local socket". `docs/permissions.md:536-539`: "any driver replies to it identically".
- `docs/configuration.md:79-81`: a repository "never sets a key that widens what runs without asking".

## The opening question: yes, for what the sandbox contains

The sandbox was measured on macOS 27.0 (Seatbelt) and Linux 6.8 (Landlock ABI 4, in Docker), alongside Claude Code's sandbox-runtime (srt) 0.0.81 and codex 0.163.0. A shell call inside the proposed sandbox (Option A below):

| can | cannot |
|---|---|
| read any file except Fiber home's `credentials/` and a person's extra denies | write outside the workspace and temp, directly or through a grandchild, `python -c` or a symlink |
| write the workspace and temp | write `.git/hooks/`, `.git/config`, a worktree's `.git` file or `.fiber/` (macOS; Linux is Q5) |
| commit in a delegate's worktree, whose git directory is outside the workspace | open any socket: no internet, no DNS, no localhost TCP, no Unix socket (so no hub, session socket, `docker.sock` or ssh-agent) |
| run and build (`cargo build` with a warm registry) | signal a process outside it (macOS; Linux from Landlock ABI 6), or ask launchd to run anything |

Each "can" is already a fast path, apart from temp writes: the read fast path reads any file except `credentials/`, and the workspace fast path writes any workspace file outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`. So **a confined call skips the reviewer as a new fast path**. The credential deny and the person's standing deny and ask rules still come first and still apply.

**Still reviewed:**

- a shell call the model marks `unconfined`, which is how it leaves the sandbox. It is judged exactly as today.
- network calls: `gh`, `git push`/`fetch`, `curl`, package installs. A domain allowlist would not contain them: allowing `github.com` allows a push to any repository, as srt's own README warns.
- writes outside the workspace: harness configuration, `~/.cargo` on a cold cache, the npm cache.
- MCP and extension tool calls, because the server or extension runs outside any shell sandbox. Codex starts MCP servers unsandboxed too (`research/sandbox/reference-agents.md`, §7).
- `delegate_*` (always reviewed), web fetches to unknown hosts, and file-tool writes outside the workspace. These are unchanged.

**How many reviews it saves.** Measured: 91% (104 of 114) in delegate lanes. Estimated: 65–83% of reviewed shell calls in the owner's interactive pi and Claude Code sessions, computed as (P − R) / (1 − R) from `research/sandbox/usage.md` (P, the share of calls that run unharmed in the sandbox) and #1497's sweep (R, the share of calls that are read-only). The two sweeps have different dates, so the second figure is an estimate. What remains is mostly `gh` and `git push`/`fetch`.

**What skipping review gives up.** Destruction inside the workspace (`rm -rf src/`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean -fdx`) runs unreviewed, and unlike an edit, it cannot be undone from the session log. Codex's workspace-write and Claude Code accept this: Claude Code's `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` "still defaults to true" in 2.1.304. See Q3.

## Options

| | **A. Fiber's own policy** (recommended) | **B. srt** | **C. bubblewrap on Linux** (codex's way) |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS | Seatbelt profile run through `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` | srt's Seatbelt profile plus an HTTP/SOCKS proxy | Seatbelt, as in A |
| Linux | Landlock plus a seccomp filter, applied in the shell's `pre_exec` | bubblewrap, socat, ripgrep, a seccomp helper, the proxy | bubblewrap with namespaces, plus seccomp |
| Added per call (median) | macOS +6 to +12 ms (the higher under load); Linux +0.3 to +0.8 ms | CLI: +100 to +184 ms (macOS). As a library: +14 ms, inside Node | Linux +1.9 ms |
| Resident while a call runs | nothing (the wrapper execs) | CLI: 76 MiB of Node per call. Library: an 85 MiB Node sidecar. Fiber's whole tree is ~35 MiB | 3.2 MiB per running command (two `bwrap` processes) |
| Starts on Ubuntu 24.04, in Docker, on GitHub's runners | yes: Landlock needs no user namespace (ABI 4 in Docker here, ABI 7 on the runners in #30) | no: failed in every Docker mode tried, and fails closed | no: needs capability-bearing user namespaces, which `apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1` and Docker's default profile refuse. Codex fails closed, so every command fails |
| Network allowlist | none: no sockets at all | yes, by domain | none, or a proxy as in B |
| Protects `.git/config`, hooks, `.fiber/` and a worktree's `.git` file | macOS: yes. Linux: no, because Landlock only grants, so a writable workspace includes them (Q5) | no `.fiber/`. On macOS the worktree's `.git` file stayed writable (measured); srt guards it on Linux only | yes (read-only binds) |

## Ruling: Linux read denies are built by enumerating ancestors (option A, with four corrections)

The contract stands: a confined shell reads everything except Fiber's credentials and the `sandbox.deny_read` paths, on Linux as on macOS. Option C would weaken the one protection the owner chose the sandbox for, on the platform that carries the usage. Option B needs unprivileged user namespaces, which Ubuntu 24.04 restricts, and a mechanism Q10 did not admit. Option D is impossible. That leaves A, built with Landlock alone.

**The mechanism.** At each confined spawn, for every denied path, Fiber walks from `/` towards it. For each existing ancestor directory on the way, it grants read on every entry except the one leading to the denied path. A directory gets a subtree grant and a file gets a file grant. The denied path itself gets nothing. Entries created in an enumerated ancestor during the call are unreadable until the next call. That fails closed.

**Corrections to the option as written:**

1. **A missing component stops the walk; it does not move the deny point up.** Treating the nearest existing ancestor as the deny point would deny all of `~` whenever `~/.aws` does not exist. Instead, the walk stops at the first missing component, and nothing is granted for it. If it is created later, it is a new entry in an enumerated directory and so unreadable. Nothing is lost, and nothing is over-denied.
2. **Never follow a symlink while building grants.** Open entries with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW`. A symlink entry gets no grant of its own. Landlock judges an access through a symlink by the target's resolved path, so the link reaches whatever its target is granted. Without this rule, a link in `~` pointing at `~/.ssh` would be opened as `~/.ssh` and granted.
3. **A denied path inside a write grant is a configuration error.** A write grant is a subtree grant, so it would re-grant reads beneath a denied path inside it. A `deny_read` path inside the workspace, the temp directory or any `allow_write` path therefore makes the sandbox unavailable for the session. One notice names the path, and the session falls back to ordinary review, as for a non-empty `allow_unix_sockets`. Fiber's credentials live in Fiber home, outside every write grant, so they always hold.
4. **Hard links are out of scope.** A hard link elsewhere to a denied file reads as that other path, on both platforms. `docs/sandbox.md` says so in one line.

**Docs (slice 1's docs commit, `docs/sandbox.md`, Linux).** State that the read set is built at spawn by enumerating the ancestors of each denied path, that entries created in those directories during a call stay unreadable until the next call, and corrections 1 to 4.

**Fence.** Yes, the walk is a helper in `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/`, already in the fence. Tests cover a denied file under `~`, with a sibling readable, a symlink to it, a missing deny path then created mid-call, and a deny path inside the workspace refused.

**Cost.** Memory is measured with the dependency measurement already required, and recorded in `docs/dependencies.md`. Spawn time adds no `docs/performance.md` row, since no shell-spawn row exists and a row needs a bench entry. The PR reports the rule count and the walk's time on Linux for the owner's home directory. If it is over a millisecond, it gets a ticket for a timing row.

| can | cannot |
|---|---|
| read any file except Fiber home's `credentials/` and a person's extra denies | write outside the workspace and temp, directly or through a grandchild, `python -c` or a symlink |
| write the workspace and temp | write `.git/hooks/`, `.git/config`, a worktree's `.git` file or `.fiber/` (macOS; Linux is Q5) |
| commit in a delegate's worktree, whose git directory is outside the workspace | open any socket: no internet, no DNS, no localhost TCP, no Unix socket (so no hub, session socket, `docker.sock` or ssh-agent) |
| run and build (`cargo build` with a warm registry) | signal a process outside it (macOS; Linux from Landlock ABI 6), or ask launchd to run anything |

Each "can" is already a fast path, apart from temp writes: the read fast path reads any file except `credentials/`, and the workspace fast path writes any workspace file outside `.git/` and `.fiber/`. - Q2: option A. Fiber writes its own policy on Seatbelt (macOS) and Landlock plus seccomp (Linux); no srt, no bubblewrap.
- Q3: keep a built-in destructive list reviewed even when confined: `rm -r`/`rm -rf`, `git reset --hard`, `git clean`, `git checkout --`, `git restore`. It matches any part of a multi-part command (unlike a standing ask rule), is checked before the confined fast path, and is best effort by command text.
- Q4: yes. With the sandbox on, read-only fast-path calls also run confined (#53's joining rule), so a wrong `shell.read_only` entry fails instead of writing. `ps` and `pgrep` fail on macOS and use the Q7 escape.
- Q5: an after-call check on Linux. Before a confined call Fiber records `.git/config`, the hooks directory, a worktree's `.git` file and `.fiber/`; after it, Fiber restores any change and reports it in the call's result. Main checkouts and worktrees are both confined.
- Q6: a confined delegate is granted all of `refs/`. A local branch moved by mistake is recovered from the reflog; `git push` stays reviewed.
- Q7: an `unconfined: true` argument on the shell tool, set by the model per call. An unconfined call is reviewed exactly as with the sandbox off. Fiber never reruns a failed confined call by itself.
- Q8: the `sandbox.*` keys are person-only, set in global config or with `-c`; a repository's project config cannot turn the sandbox on. A delegate inherits its parent's setting. A `/sandbox` command is part of this design: it turns the sandbox on or off for the running session. Toggling changes the shell tool's description, a person-initiated prompt-cache miss, which is acceptable.
- Q9: a new area doc, `docs/sandbox.md`, holds the per-platform policy (Seatbelt profile, Landlock grants, seccomp, the Linux after-call check, worktree grants). `docs/permissions.md` "Confinement" states the rule and links to it.
- Q10: the `landlock` and `seccompiler` crates, admitted through `docs/dependencies.md` with their memory measured. Floor Landlock ABI 2 (Linux 5.19); below it the sandbox reports unavailable and calls are reviewed.
- Q11: yes. "Sandbox" names the feature and its keys; "confined" names a call that ran inside it.

## Ruling: Linux read denies are built by enumerating ancestors (option A, with four corrections)

The contract stands: a confined shell reads everything except Fiber's credentials and the `sandbox.deny_read` paths, on Linux as on macOS. Option C would weaken the one protection the owner chose the sandbox for, on the platform that carries the usage. Option B needs unprivileged user namespaces, which Ubuntu 24.04 restricts, and a mechanism Q10 did not admit. Option D is impossible. That leaves A, built with Landlock alone.

**The mechanism.** At each confined spawn, for every denied path, Fiber walks from `/` towards it. For each existing ancestor directory on the way, it grants read on every entry except the one leading to the denied path. A directory gets a subtree grant and a file gets a file grant. The denied path itself gets nothing. Entries created in an enumerated ancestor during the call are unreadable until the next call. That fails closed.

**Corrections to the option as written:**

1. **A missing component stops the walk; it does not move the deny point up.** Treating the nearest existing ancestor as the deny point would deny all of `~` whenever `~/.aws` does not exist. Instead, the walk stops at the first missing component, and nothing is granted for it. If it is created later, it is a new entry in an enumerated directory and so unreadable. Nothing is lost, and nothing is over-denied.
2. **Never follow a symlink while building grants.** Open entries with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW`. A symlink entry gets no grant of its own. Landlock judges an access through a symlink by the target's resolved path, so the link reaches whatever its target is granted. Without this rule, a link in `~` pointing at `~/.ssh` would be opened as `~/.ssh` and granted.
3. **A denied path inside a write grant is a configuration error.** A write grant is a subtree grant, so it would re-grant reads beneath a denied path inside it. A `deny_read` path inside the workspace, the temp directory or any `allow_write` path therefore makes the sandbox unavailable for the session. One notice names the path, and the session falls back to ordinary review, as for a non-empty `allow_unix_sockets`. Fiber's credentials live in Fiber home, outside every write grant, so they always hold.
4. **Hard links are out of scope.** A hard link elsewhere to a denied file reads as that other path, on both platforms. `docs/sandbox.md` says so in one line.

**Docs (slice 1's docs commit, `docs/sandbox.md`, Linux).** State that the read set is built at spawn by enumerating the ancestors of each denied path, that entries created in those directories during a call stay unreadable until the next call, and corrections 1 to 4.

**Fence.** Yes, the walk is a helper in `crates/tools/src/shell/sandbox/`, already in the fence. Tests cover a denied file under `~`, with a sibling readable, a symlink to it, a missing deny path then created mid-call, and a deny path inside the workspace refused.

**Cost.** Memory is measured with the dependency measurement already required, and recorded in `docs/dependencies.md`. Spawn time adds no `docs/performance.md` row, since no shell-spawn row exists and a row needs a bench entry. The PR reports the rule count and the walk's time on Linux for the owner's home directory. If it is over a millisecond, it gets a ticket for a timing row.

Give each shell command that builds or runs tests a timeout of at least 600 seconds; a shorter limit kills the run partway and reads as a failure.

An additive edit to an existing file outside it (a new enum variant, match arm, struct field, `mod` line, slash-table entry, test function or docs section) is allowed: add lines only, delete none, and list each such file in your report; the second PR to merge takes main and resolves. Before pushing, check the branch's whole diff against it: `git diff --name-only --no-renames origin/main...HEAD`, which lists a renamed file under its old path as well. A file outside Files must already exist on main and show zero deleted lines in `git diff --numstat origin/main...HEAD -- <path>`.
- Before the first task, check the plan against 69bfbe701ef5988bb58e048cb361791dd0e955a9, which may be newer than the plan: every path it names that the plan does not create exists (`git cat-file -e HEAD:<path>`), and `git grep -n` finds every existing function, type, constant and test it names, tests in every crate or package included. A miss means main moved under the plan: stop and report each miss with what main has in its place.
- Every acceptance criterion and doc requirement the ticket names ships. When one can't, stop and report it as a design question.
- Stop and report before you add or change a public interface the plan's Interfaces don't list, delete or weaken a test or doc sentence you did not add, loosen any test's timeout, wait, retry count or numeric tolerance (your own tests included) that neither the plan nor the ticket's acceptance criteria call for, or add a dependency. For a looser bound, report the cause it would hide.
- When the code makes a plan ruling wrong or unworkable, stop and report it with the evidence; build no alternative.
- Run the tasks in order, each test first, and pass each task's gate and commit before starting the next.
- Run only the gate and the tests your tasks name. Suites the workflow doc gives to CI, such as mutation testing (`cargo mutants`), benchmarks and backstops, run in CI: read their result from the CI log, and report when you need one reproduced.
- Run every command in the foreground, so it ends before your turn does; start no background or detached process. When the gate outlasts one tool call, run the narrowest test set your change reaches in the foreground and leave the full gate to the job-end gate. The pi harness turns a command still running after 30s into a job it manages, which is not a detached process: wait on it with the `jobs` tool, `action: "wait"`, its id and `timeout: 3600`, and repeat until it ends. Don't poll its log; bare `sleep` is blocked.
- A look or probe task (running the program or a TUI to see what it does) gets 3 probe rounds. Then end with `STATUS: NEEDS_CONTEXT` and a verdict digest: what each round showed and what stays unknown.
- Run every command in your worktree, each one starting `cd $HOME/work/fiber-worktrees/ci/3088-flake-issue-commit &&`: a shell's working directory can reset between calls, and a build or test run elsewhere lands in another agent's checkout. - Commit each new script under `bin/` as executable: `chmod 755` it, then `git ls-files -s <path>` shows mode `100755`.
- Mark a deliberate shortcut with a `debt: <ceiling>, <upgrade trigger>` comment. A shortcut that would weaken a rule a doc, spec or ticket states gets no marker: stop and report.
- Commit your work before any command that discards changes (`git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- <path>`, `git restore`, a rebase). Make a scratch commit, such as one kept as evidence, on a throwaway branch (`git switch -c scratch/<name>`), then switch back to the lane branch and delete the scratch one.
- Give each new comparison, match guard and `&&`/`||` condition a test that fails when it flips: for a comparison, values at, just below and just above the edge. See each new assert fail against deliberately broken code before you rely on it.
- A test asserts behaviour: pin a fixture by a tag or by the repo it builds, never by a commit sha, which a rebase rewrites.
- Give each blocking wait in a test you add (a join, a `recv`, an attempt-count loop) a deadline, so a bug fails the test instead of hanging it.
- Write comments that state the rule itself, never "ruling N" or "per the plan".
- When the plan names a Red commit, make it the branch's first commit, holding only those files.
- To rebuild the branch's history, reset to the merge-base (`git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)`), never to `origin/main` and never with `git checkout <branch> -- .`: both drop main's newer changes.
- Set work aside with a commit. To compare against main, build main in a throwaway worktree (`git worktree add --detach ../cmp-<branch> origin/main`, then `git worktree remove` it). Only a worktree or branch you created is yours to remove: the shared checkout is never a target of `git worktree remove` or `git branch -D`, and `ship-pr` cleans up your own worktree when you run it from outside that worktree. Then the PR URL and its head SHA with the gate's last output line quoted from its log (report a pass only beside a log that ends in one), or a failure triage (the step, the command, its output tail), nothing in between. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# The self-test for the flake report's write step (.github/workflows/ci.yml,
# job flake_report; docs/testing/running.md, "Flaky tests"). It runs that
# step's own script, cut from the workflow file, against a stub `gh` that
# records each write and answers each read from the case's fixture. Every
# write path is proven: a new issue, a comment on an open issue, and a pull
# request comment for a failing file the pull request owns. Each body names
# the tested commit: `tested <sha> = main <base> + head <head>` on a pull
# request run with two parents, and `tested <sha>` on a push run or a pull
# request run with one parent. Nothing reaches the GitHub API.
#
# Usage: scripts/test-flake-report
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT

fail() {
  echo "scripts/test-flake-report: $1" >&2
  exit 1
}

# The step is the one whose name is given below: its `run: |` block, every
# line indented past the `run:` key. No YAML parser: the name is unique.
awk '
  index($0, "- name: File or comment on the flake issues") { armed = 1; next }
  armed && !started && $0 ~ /^ *run: \|$/ { started = 1; match($0, /[^ ]/); indent = RSTART - 1; next }
  started {
    if ($0 ~ /^ *$/) { print ""; next }
    match($0, /[^ ]/)
    if (RSTART - 1 <= indent) exit
    print
  }
' .github/workflows/ci.yml >"$tmp/step.sh"
grep -Fq 'flake_body() {' "$tmp/step.sh" || fail "the flake report step's script was not found in .github/workflows/ci.yml"

# The stub, written ahead of the step so it needs no executable on PATH.
# A write becomes one file, numbered in order: its first line is `create
# <title>` or `comment <number>`, the rest is the body exactly.
cat >"$tmp/stub.sh" <<'EOF'
gh() {
  case "$1" in
    api)
      case "$*" in
        *"/commits/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_PARENTS" ;;
        *"/compare/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_COMPARE" ;;
        *"/pulls/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_PR_FILES" ;;
        *) echo "stub gh: unexpected api call: $*" >&2; return 1 ;;
      esac
      ;;
    issue)
      verb=$2
      shift 2
      case "$verb" in
        list) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_NUMBER"; return 0 ;;
        comment) header="comment $1"; shift ;;
        create) header="create" ;;
        *) echo "stub gh: unexpected issue verb: $verb" >&2; return 1 ;;
      esac
      title=""
      body=""
      while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
          --title) title=$2 ;;
          --body) body=$2 ;;
          *) echo "stub gh: unexpected argument: $1" >&2; return 1 ;;
        esac
        shift 2
      done
      [ "$verb" = create ] && header="create $title"
      n=$(ls -A "$STUB_CALLS" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
      printf '%s\n%s' "$header" "$body" >"$STUB_CALLS/$n"
      ;;
    *) echo "stub gh: unexpected call: $*" >&2; return 1 ;;
  esac
}
EOF
cat "$tmp/stub.sh" "$tmp/step.sh" >"$tmp/run.sh"

sha=1111111111111111111111111111111111111111
base=2222222222222222222222222222222222222222
head=3333333333333333333333333333333333333333
url=https://github.example/aakshintala/fiber/actions/runs/1
name='main::flaky_probe fails_once_then_passes'
title="Flaky test: $name"
detail='thread fails_once_then_passes panicked at crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs:10:9\nfirst attempt'
fence='```'

# run_case CASE EVENT PR PARENTS COMPARE PR_FILES NUMBER WANT: runs the step
# on one flake and checks the one write against WANT.
run_case() {
  dir=$tmp/$1
  mkdir -p "$dir/temp/flaky" "$dir/calls"
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$name" "$detail" >"$dir/temp/flaky/flaky-tests-linux.txt"
  env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$dir" \
    RUNNER_TEMP="$dir/temp" GITHUB_SHA="$sha" GITHUB_EVENT_NAME="$2" \
    GITHUB_RUN_ID=1 GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY="$dir/summary" \
    GH_REPO=aakshintala/fiber GH_TOKEN=test RUN_URL="$url" PR="$3" \
    STUB_PARENTS="$4" STUB_COMPARE="$5" STUB_PR_FILES="$6" STUB_NUMBER="$7" \
    STUB_CALLS="$dir/calls" \
    bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail "$tmp/run.sh" 2>"$dir/err" || fail "$1: the step exited $?"
  [ -s "$dir/err" ] && { cat "$dir/err" >&2; fail "$1: the step printed to stderr"; }
  [ "$(ls -A "$dir/calls" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')" -eq 1 ] || fail "$1: want one write, got $(ls -A "$dir/calls" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
  got=$(cat "$dir/calls/0")
  [ "$got" = "$8" ] || {
    echo "--- want:" >&2
    printf '%s\n' "$8" >&2
    echo "--- got:" >&2
    printf '%s\n' "$got" >&2
    fail "$1: the write differs"
  }
}

push_tested="tested $sha"
pr_tested="tested $sha = main $base + head $head"
plain="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux: $url."
see_pr="$plain (see #12)"
belongs="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux, but its failing file \`crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs\` belongs to #12 rather than main: $url."

# The body is the sentence, the tested line, then the failure in a fence.
body() {
  printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n%s\n%s' "$1" "$2" "$fence" "$detail" "$fence"
}

# A push run: a new issue, then a comment on the open one.
run_case push-create push "" "" "" "" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"
run_case push-comment push "" "" "" "" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"

# A pull request run with two parents, main then the pull request head: a new
# issue naming the pull request, a comment on the open one, and a comment for
# a failing file the pull request changed.
run_case pr-create pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-sighting pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-comment pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs" "" "$(printf 'comment 12\n%s' "$(body "$belongs" "$pr_tested")")"

# A pull request run whose commit has one parent falls back to the push line.
run_case pr-one-parent pull_request 12 "$base" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$push_tested")")"

echo "scripts/test-flake-report: ok"

When the finding is wrong, leave the code and answer it with evidence: a test, a call site, a command's output. A finding that names a pattern a test relies on (a real-clock hold, a `sleep`, a fixed wait) is a class: search the PR's diff for that pattern and remove it from every test the PR adds or changes. Leave code the PR didn't touch. A compile fix a rebase forces belongs to the rebase, not to a finding.
- Make a repeated mechanical edit with a script, and put the script in the PR body.
- An over-engineering finding is a hypothesis: apply it only when the cut costs no memory, behaviour or lines.

- Keep every test's timeouts, waits, retry counts and numeric tolerances as they are. A fix that needs a looser one stops and reports the cause it would hide.
- When the same check fails twice after your fixes, stop: report the assumption your fixes share, and start no third patch.

- A test that kills a mutant CI reported is in scope: list it with the findings.
- Each comparison, condition or branch your fix adds gets a test that fails when it flips; name that test in your report beside its finding.
- A test asserts behaviour: pin a fixture by a tag or by the repo it builds, never by a commit sha, which a rebase rewrites.

CI's mutant lines refer to the head CI ran; once a commit moves code, find each mutant by its function and replacement.

# The self-test for the flake report's write step (.github/workflows/ci.yml,
# job flake_report; docs/testing/running.md, "Flaky tests"). It runs that
# step's own script, cut from the workflow file, against a stub `gh` that
# records each write and answers each read from the case's fixture. Every
# write path is proven: a new issue, a comment on an open issue, and a pull
# request comment for a failing file the pull request owns. Each body names
# the tested commit: `tested <sha> = main <base> + head <head>` on a pull
# request run with two parents, and `tested <sha>` on a push run or a pull
# request run with one parent. Nothing reaches the GitHub API.
#
# Usage: scripts/test-flake-report
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

tmp=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT

fail() {
  echo "scripts/test-flake-report: $1" >&2
  exit 1
}

# The step is the one whose name is given below: its `run: |` block, every
# line indented past the `run:` key. No YAML parser: the name is unique.
awk '
  index($0, "- name: File or comment on the flake issues") { armed = 1; next }
  armed && !started && $0 ~ /^ *run: \|$/ { started = 1; match($0, /[^ ]/); indent = RSTART - 1; next }
  started {
    if ($0 ~ /^ *$/) { print ""; next }
    match($0, /[^ ]/)
    if (RSTART - 1 <= indent) exit
    print
  }
' .github/workflows/ci.yml >"$tmp/step.sh"
grep -Fq 'flake_body() {' "$tmp/step.sh" || fail "the flake report step's script was not found in .github/workflows/ci.yml"

# The stub, written ahead of the step so it needs no executable on PATH.
# A write becomes one file, numbered in order: its first line is `create
# <title>` or `comment <number>`, the rest is the body exactly.
cat >"$tmp/stub.sh" <<'EOF'
gh() {
  case "$1" in
    api)
      case "$*" in
        *"/commits/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_PARENTS" ;;
        *"/compare/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_COMPARE" ;;
        *"/pulls/"*) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_PR_FILES" ;;
        *) echo "stub gh: unexpected api call: $*" >&2; return 1 ;;
      esac
      ;;
    issue)
      verb=$2
      shift 2
      case "$verb" in
        list) printf '%s\n' "$STUB_NUMBER"; return 0 ;;
        comment) header="comment $1"; shift ;;
        create) header="create" ;;
        *) echo "stub gh: unexpected issue verb: $verb" >&2; return 1 ;;
      esac
      title=""
      body=""
      while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
          --title) title=$2 ;;
          --body) body=$2 ;;
          *) echo "stub gh: unexpected argument: $1" >&2; return 1 ;;
        esac
        shift 2
      done
      [ "$verb" = create ] && header="create $title"
      n=$(ls -A "$STUB_CALLS" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')
      printf '%s\n%s' "$header" "$body" >"$STUB_CALLS/$n"
      ;;
    *) echo "stub gh: unexpected call: $*" >&2; return 1 ;;
  esac
}
EOF
cat "$tmp/stub.sh" "$tmp/step.sh" >"$tmp/run.sh"

sha=1111111111111111111111111111111111111111
base=2222222222222222222222222222222222222222
head=3333333333333333333333333333333333333333
url=https://github.example/aakshintala/fiber/actions/runs/1
name='main::flaky_probe fails_once_then_passes'
title="Flaky test: $name"
detail='thread fails_once_then_passes panicked at crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs:10:9\nfirst attempt'
fence='```'

# run_case CASE EVENT PR PARENTS COMPARE PR_FILES NUMBER WANT: runs the step
# on one flake and checks the one write against WANT.
run_case() {
  dir=$tmp/$1
  mkdir -p "$dir/temp/flaky" "$dir/calls"
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$name" "$detail" >"$dir/temp/flaky/flaky-tests-linux.txt"
  env -i PATH="$PATH" HOME="$dir" \
    RUNNER_TEMP="$dir/temp" GITHUB_SHA="$sha" GITHUB_EVENT_NAME="$2" \
    GITHUB_RUN_ID=1 GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY="$dir/summary" \
    GH_REPO=aakshintala/fiber GH_TOKEN=test RUN_URL="$url" PR="$3" \
    STUB_PARENTS="$4" STUB_COMPARE="$5" STUB_PR_FILES="$6" STUB_NUMBER="$7" \
    STUB_CALLS="$dir/calls" \
    bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail "$tmp/run.sh" 2>"$dir/err" || fail "$1: the step exited $?"
  [ -s "$dir/err" ] && { cat "$dir/err" >&2; fail "$1: the step printed to stderr"; }
  [ "$(ls -A "$dir/calls" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')" -eq 1 ] || fail "$1: want one write, got $(ls -A "$dir/calls" | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
  got=$(cat "$dir/calls/0")
  [ "$got" = "$8" ] || {
    echo "--- want:" >&2
    printf '%s\n' "$8" >&2
    echo "--- got:" >&2
    printf '%s\n' "$got" >&2
    fail "$1: the write differs"
  }
}

push_tested="tested $sha"
pr_tested="tested $sha = main $base + head $head"
plain="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux: $url."
see_pr="$plain (see #12)"
belongs="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux, but its failing file \`crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs\` belongs to #12 rather than main: $url."

# The body is the sentence, the tested line, then the failure in a fence.
body() {
  printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n%s\n%s' "$1" "$2" "$fence" "$detail" "$fence"
}

# A push run: a new issue, then a comment on the open one.
run_case push-create push "" "" "" "" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"
run_case push-comment push "" "" "" "" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"

# A pull request run with two parents, main then the pull request head: a new
# issue naming the pull request, a comment on the open one, and a comment for
# a failing file the pull request changed.
run_case pr-create pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-sighting pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-comment pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs" "" "$(printf 'comment 12\n%s' "$(body "$belongs" "$pr_tested")")"

# A pull request run whose commit has one parent falls back to the push line.
run_case pr-one-parent pull_request 12 "$base" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$push_tested")")"

echo "scripts/test-flake-report: ok"

## Findings

P2 .github/workflows/ci.yml:842 — CI actionlint's shellcheck reports SC2016 in the changed flake_report script: `Expressions don't expand in single quotes, use double quotes for that`. Resolve the exact lint in the workflow script and verify with actionlint 1.7.12.

Add a deterministic probe that runs in PR CI, proving push and PR formats and each write path, and have the PR body link its CI log. Update the PR body so it no longer describes the stub probe as the only exercise.


## Rules

- Check each finding against the code before acting. Fix it when the code shows the defect. When the finding is wrong, leave the code and answer it with evidence: a test, a call site, a command's output. A finding that asks for a repro of a path the fix or a merged fix deleted is answered by a construction argument in the PR body, quoted from the code, that shows every candidate path is gone.
- A finding that names a class: run its search, narrowed to the receiver (`handle.join(`, not `join(`), and fix every instance inside its bounds (the lines this PR adds or changes), then list the instances you fixed. A finding that names a pattern a test relies on (a real-clock hold, a `sleep`, a fixed wait) is a class: search the PR's diff for that pattern and remove it from every test the PR adds or changes. Leave code the PR didn't touch. A compile fix a rebase forces belongs to the rebase, not to a finding.
- Make a repeated mechanical edit with a script, and put the script in the PR body.
- An over-engineering finding is a hypothesis: apply it only when the cut costs no memory, behaviour or lines.
- Stay inside the fence: .github/workflows/ci.yml — change only the flake_report job's body construction and its three writes.
scripts/flaky-tests — raise the detail limit to 6000 and update its comment.
scripts/test-flaky-tests — pin full 6000-character output and truncation above the limit.
docs/testing/running.md — document the tested-commit line and 6000-character cap under Flaky tests.. When you need to rewrite code in a file outside it, stop and report; an additive edit to an existing file (a new enum variant, match arm, struct field, `mod` line, slash-table entry, test function or docs section) is allowed. A change to a test harness or fixture that more than the finding uses is checked against the ticket's scope note first; when it goes past the note, stop and report `NEEDS_CONTEXT`.
- Mark a deliberate shortcut with a `debt: <ceiling>, <upgrade trigger>` comment. A shortcut that would weaken a rule a doc, spec or ticket states gets no marker: stop and report.
- Keep every test's timeouts, waits, retry counts and numeric tolerances as they are. A fix that needs a looser one stops and reports the cause it would hide.
- When the same check fails twice after your fixes, stop: report the assumption your fixes share, and start no third patch.
- Refer to issues as `see #N` or `#N's case` in commit messages; a closing keyword (close, fix, resolve and their forms) before an issue number closes that issue on merge.
- Commit your work before any command that discards changes (`git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- <path>`, `git restore`, a rebase). Make a scratch commit, such as one kept as evidence, on a throwaway branch (`git switch -c scratch/<name>`), then switch back to the lane branch and delete the scratch one.

- Each comparison, condition or branch your fix adds gets a test that fails when it flips; name that test in your report beside its finding.

Otherwise apply the exemption rule and written reason of the workflow doc or the testing doc it names (`exempted: <reason>`); with no such rule, remove it. CI fails until one lands; never report it as equivalent alone.

When the gate outlasts one tool call, run the narrowest test set your change reaches in the foreground and leave the full gate to the job-end gate. The pi harness turns a command still running after 30s into a job it manages, which is not a detached process: wait on it with the `jobs` tool, `action: "wait"`, its id and `timeout: 3600`, and repeat until it ends. Don't poll its log; bare `sleep` is blocked.
- Set work aside with a commit. The stash stack is shared with every other worktree of the repo, so `git stash` can pop another agent's changes.

Push once, with every fix from this round, once the required checks on the head you started from have all passed or one has failed: `~/.agents/bin/gh-ci wait 3100 --repo aakshintala/fiber --fail-fast --timeout <s>` waits for that, with `<s>` a multiple of 30 at least 60 s under your shell's per-command limit, since the wait overshoots its timeout by up to one 30 s poll plus its API calls (60 when you don't know the limit); on exit 124, or when the shell cuts the wait off, run the same wait again, and push only after it exits 0 or 1. plain="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux: $url."

belongs="The test \`$name\` passed after a retry on linux, but its failing file \`crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs\` belongs to #12 rather than main: $url."

# The body is the sentence, the tested line, then the failure in a fence.
body() {
  printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n%s\n%s' "$1" "$2" "$fence" "$detail" "$fence"
}

# A push run: a new issue, then a comment on the open one.
run_case push-create push "" "" "" "" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"
run_case push-comment push "" "" "" "" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$plain" "$push_tested")")"

# A pull request run with two parents, main then the pull request head: a new
# issue naming the pull request, a comment on the open one, and a comment for
# a failing file the pull request changed.
run_case pr-create pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-sighting pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "other/file.rs" 7 "$(printf 'comment 7\n%s' "$(body "$see_pr" "$pr_tested")")"
run_case pr-comment pull_request 12 "$base $head" "" "crates/main/tests/flaky_probe.rs" "" "$(printf 'comment 12\n%s' "$(body "$belongs" "$pr_tested")")"

# A pull request run whose commit has one parent falls back to the push line.
run_case pr-one-parent pull_request 12 "$base" "" "other/file.rs" "" "$(printf 'create %s\n%s' "$title" "$(body "$see_pr" "$push_tested")")"

Answer the review findings on PR #3171 in aakshintala/fiber, in worktree `$HOME/work/fiber-worktrees/cli/2863-feedback-diagnostics` on branch `cli/2863-feedback-diagnostics`. Do not delegate further.

The project's workflow doc is $HOME/work/fiber-worktrees/cli/2863-feedback-diagnostics/docs/workflow.md; it wins where it speaks.

## Findings

VERDICT standards: CHANGES
P2 crates/contract/src/feedback.rs:14 — The feedback seam passes a session identifier as `Option<&str>`, and the TUI strips `SessionId` to a string before calling it. This breaks the rule that each kind of identifier has its own newtype (`docs/code-quality.md`, “Types”). Keep `SessionId` typed across the seam and diagnostics APIs.
P2 crates/main/src/main.rs:662 — `feedback_session` implements feedback-specific session selection and delegate validation in `main`, contrary to its composition-root rule: “No feature logic” (`docs/architecture.md`, module table). Move this behavior into `cli`; let `main` dispatch it.

VERDICT spec: CHANGES
P1 crates/cli/src/feedback.rs:219 — `entry()` accepts a `debug` line without checking that `data` is an object, then copies the raw JSON line into the report. An invalid line can therefore carry arbitrary content into the attachment, contrary to the plan’s rule that a debug line has “`data`, an object of named values” and that uncertain lines are omitted — validate the debug field shape before copying the line.

VERDICT overbuild: CHANGES
P3 crates/tui/src/app/commands_tests.rs:998 — delete — cut `feedback_hands_the_writer_the_attached_session`, which calls `feedback::start` by hand and re-asserts what `feedback_tests.rs:48` and the existing `app.session()` tests already pin — replace with nothing
P3 crates/cli/src/feedback.rs:47 — yagni — cut `FeedbackError::Diagnostics`, its `From` arm and `feedback_tests.rs:434`, since the only production capturer always returns `Ok` — replace with an infallible `Fn(Option<&str>) -> String`
P3 crates/cli/src/feedback.rs:239 — shrink — cut `newest`'s `favour` flag and the dropped count the hub caller discards at :380 — replace with `sort_by_key`, then `drain(..len.saturating_sub(HUB_LINES))` for the hub; keep `newest` for the session's priority cap
P3 crates/cli/src/feedback.rs:225 — stdlib — cut the hand-rolled byte split with `from_utf8` per line — replace with `fs::read_to_string(path)` and `.lines()`


## Rules

- Check each finding against the code before acting. Fix it when the code shows the defect. When the finding is wrong, leave the code and answer it with evidence: a test, a call site, a command's output. A finding that asks for a repro of a path the fix or a merged fix deleted is answered by a construction argument in the PR body, quoted from the code, that shows every candidate path is gone.
- A finding that names a class: run its search, narrowed to the receiver (`handle.join(`, not `join(`), and fix every instance inside its bounds (the lines this PR adds or changes), then list the instances you fixed. A finding that names a pattern a test relies on (a real-clock hold, a `sleep`, a fixed wait) is a class: search the PR's diff for that pattern and remove it from every test the PR adds or changes. Leave code the PR didn't touch. A compile fix a rebase forces belongs to the rebase, not to a finding.
- Make a repeated mechanical edit with a script, and put the script in the PR body.
- An over-engineering finding is a hypothesis: apply it only when the cut costs no memory, behaviour or lines.
- Stay inside the fence: crates/cli/src/feedback.rs: diagnostics capture/rendering, safe log/crash filtering, cap and link exclusion; typed session selection; infallible diagnostics capture; JSON debug-data object validation; remove overbuilt helper branches as ruled.
crates/cli/src/feedback_tests.rs: filtering, links, crash extraction, hub stream/window/cap, session cap/priority/ties and notices using FakeClock; debug data shape tests for string, array, null and object; remove the ruled infallible-capturer error test.

crates/main/src/cli_tests.rs: additive parser tests for valid and malformed ids.
crates/main/src/main.rs: parse feedback args and dispatch; no feedback session-selection or delegate-validation logic. Pass typed session id through the TUI writer closure.
crates/main/tests/feedback.rs: binary fake-home privacy repro; assert diagnostics/backtrace, no marker, link exclusion, explicit missing id and default session.
crates/main/tests/completion.rs: expectation-only update for the new CLI flag; outside-fence expectation update, list in PR body.
crates/main/tests/ask.rs: expectation-only update to the hard-coded help menu for the new CLI flag; outside-fence expectation update, list in PR body.
crates/tui/src/feedback.rs: pass typed active session id through writer seam without stringifying it.
crates/tui/src/feedback_tests.rs: assert writer gets current session id.
crates/tui/src/event_loop.rs: only granted Effect::Feedback hunk supplies active id.

When you need to rewrite code in a file outside it, stop and report; an additive edit to an existing file (a new enum variant, match arm, struct field, `mod` line, slash-table entry, test function or docs section) is allowed. A change to a test harness or fixture that more than the finding uses is checked against the ticket's scope note first; when it goes past the note, stop and report `NEEDS_CONTEXT`.
- Mark a deliberate shortcut with a `debt: <ceiling>, <upgrade trigger>` comment. A shortcut that would weaken a rule a doc, spec or ticket states gets no marker: stop and report.
- Keep every test's timeouts, waits, retry counts and numeric tolerances as they are. A fix that needs a looser one stops and reports the cause it would hide.
- When the same check fails twice after your fixes, stop: report the assumption your fixes share, and start no third patch.
- Refer to issues as `see #N` or `#N's case` in commit messages; a closing keyword (close, fix, resolve and their forms) before an issue number closes that issue on merge.
- Commit your work before any command that discards changes (`git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- <path>`, `git restore`, a rebase). Make a scratch commit, such as one kept as evidence, on a throwaway branch (`git switch -c scratch/<name>`), then switch back to the lane branch and delete the scratch one.
- A test that kills a mutant CI reported is in scope: list it with the findings.
- Each comparison, condition or branch your fix adds gets a test that fails when it flips; name that test in your report beside its finding.
- A test asserts behaviour: pin a fixture by a tag or by the repo it builds, never by a commit sha, which a rebase rewrites.
